 Follow There’s a voter ID measure on California’s midterm ballot. What to know about Prop. 39
 Kiara Adams, video script produced using AI assistance Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:32 AM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. An American flag decorates a privacy booth at a polling station during the first day of early voting for the midterm elections in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on Oct, 16, 2026. Americans voting in the November 3 midterm elections will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency, along with dozens of governorships and thousands of state offices. Proposition 39 tightens voter identification requirements for in-person and mail-in ballots in California. Below is a transcript of the video above. Read our voter guide story on Prop. 39 here , along with the editorial board's take on the issue . 
 There's a measure on your California ballot that could change how you vote. It's called Proposition 39. Let's talk about it.
 If Prop. 39 passes, you'd have to show a government-issued photo ID every time you vote in person. Voting by mail? You'd write the last four digits of an ID number — your driver's license, for example — on the return envelope.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Don't have an ID? The state would be required to give you a free voter ID card, no charge, if you ask for one.
 There's a second piece, too. Election officials would have to use government data to check that registered voters are U.S. citizens, then publish those results every year.
 So who's behind this? Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio is leading the charge. He calls it a commonsense fix to rebuild trust in elections. The yes campaign has pulled in more than $24 million, a lot of it from right-leaning billionaires .
 On the other side: Democrats like Governor Gavin Newsom and Nancy Pelosi , as well as voting rights groups. They argue it would keep eligible people from voting to solve a problem — in-person voter fraud — that research shows is extremely rare.
 Advertisement Advertisement Implementing voter ID won't be cheap either. State analysts estimate it would cost tens of millions dollars — or even hundreds of millions — every year.
 This November, it's up to you. Yes or No on Prop 39.
